bodies.name: 3I/ATLAS
bodies.periodText: At least about 1 hour; not determined
bodies.credit: Hui, Jewitt, Mutchler, Agarwal and Kim (2026), ApJL, Hubble WFC3 nucleus photometry (arXiv:2601.21569)
bodies.shapeMeaning: Hubble photometry gives an effective radius of 1.3 ± 0.2 km, assuming V-band geometric albedo 0.04, and brightness changes of at least 0.8 mag imply a sky-plane axis ratio of 2:1 or more. No shape model, pole or period was published. This display is a prolate ellipsoid at exactly the minimum 2:1 ratio, sized so the geometric mean of its largest and smallest cross-sections equals π × (1.3 km)²: full axes 4.37 × 2.19 × 2.19 km. A longer body, another albedo or a different shape would change it.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Arbitrary display pole and meridian. No rotation pole or phase has been measured.
bodies.introduction: It swung past the Sun in October 2025. Hubble later picked out its nucleus from the dust; the shape shown is elongated to match that brightness, not an image.
bodies.card: The third interstellar object seen passing through the Solar System.
bodies.datasetSummary: An elongated body sized from Hubble brightness with an assumed dark surface; the true shape is unknown.
survey: Included: Hui et al. (2026) Hubble WFC3 photometry, December 2025 to January 2026: effective radius 1.3 ± 0.2 km at pV 0.04 and axis ratio at least 2:1.
Superseded for size: Jewitt et al. (2025) July 2025 Hubble images, which limited the radius to at most 2.8 km while dust hid the nucleus.
Excluded: artist impressions and coma photographs as surface textures; the nucleus is unresolved.
Included: JPL Horizons 2026-09-03 heliocentric osculating trajectory and independent vectors; not a simulation of its non-gravitational acceleration.

bodies.name: 2I/Borisov
bodies.credit: Hui, Ye, Föhring, Hung and Tholen (2020), AJ 160, 92, nucleus size from non-gravitational acceleration
bodies.shapeMeaning: No image resolves the nucleus. Hubble limits its radius to at most 0.5 km at assumed geometric albedo 0.04, and its non-gravitational acceleration requires at least 0.2 km at assumed density 500 kg/m³ (Jewitt et al. 2020). Hui et al. (2020) estimate it is most likely at most 0.4 km. The display is a 0.4 km sphere: an estimate inside those bounds, not a measured size or shape.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Pole RA 205°, Dec 52° (obliquity 30°), fitted to coma anisotropy by Kim et al. (2020); the prime meridian and spin phase are arbitrary and the period is not determined.
bodies.introduction: It swung past the Sun in December 2019, trailing gas like an ordinary comet. Its nucleus was never resolved; the sphere shown is an estimated size.
bodies.card: The second interstellar object seen passing through the Solar System, and the first clearly active comet.
bodies.datasetSummary: A sphere of estimated size inside Hubble limits, turned on the pole fitted to its coma; the true shape is unknown.
survey: Included: Hui et al. (2020) nucleus radius most likely at most 0.4 km from non-gravitational acceleration and CO production.
Included as bounds: Jewitt et al. (2020) Hubble coma modelling, radius at most 0.5 km (pV 0.04), and at least 0.2 km from acceleration (density 500 kg/m³).
Included: Kim et al. (2020) pole RA 205°, Dec 52° from coma anisotropy.
Excluded: coma photographs and artist impressions as surface textures; the nucleus is unresolved. The 2020 outburst fragments are not modelled.
Included: JPL Horizons 2026-09-03 heliocentric osculating trajectory and independent vectors.
